title: Interactive regressions & specification curve
Interactive regressions & specification curve
text:
What is being estimated?
For each combination of analytic choices below, we estimate a panel regression of the form
\[
\text{lib}^{(d)}_{p,c,t} \;=\; \beta\,\text{pop}_{p,c,t} \;+\; \mu_c \;+\; \mu_t \;+\; \varepsilon_{p,c,t}
\]
where the observation is one party \(p\) × country \(c\) × election year \(t\) manifesto. \(\text{pop}_{p,c,t}\) is the populism-overall score for that manifesto (averaged across LLMs and chunks per the selected aggregation), and \(\text{lib}^{(d)}_{p,c,t}\) is the score on the chosen liberalism dimension \(d\). The fixed effects \(\mu_c, \mu_t\) absorb everything country-constant and year-constant; standard errors are clustered by party. The coefficient of interest is \(\beta\) — the partial association between populism and liberalism, holding country and year fixed.

How the forks change \(\beta\)








Fork
What varies
Why it might matter




Model selection
Which LLM(s) produce the scores (Sonnet, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini, or any combination)
Different models may disagree systematically; restricting to one tests sensitivity to the LLM “voice”


Within-manifesto aggregation
How chunks of one manifesto combine into a single score (confidence-weighted mean, plain mean, median)
Long manifestos get split into chunks; the way we collapse them matters


Between-model aggregation
How three LLM scores merge into a cross-model score (mean, median, leave-worst-out)
Disagreement weighting changes the consensus


Outcome dimension
Which liberalism dimension is the dependent variable
Effects may be stronger for some sub-dimensions (e.g. financial-market) than others


Sample restriction
Which manifestos enter the regression (all years, post-2000, post-2010, Europe-only)
Tests historical and geographic robustness


Fixed effects
Country + year, + party, or country × year interactions
Tighter FE absorb more unobserved heterogeneity


Evidence rule
Which chunk scores count: quote check (quote, baseline); plus a topic check for the ideology and overall dimensions (r12); quote and topic checks for all dimensions (full); no span filter (none)
Tests how much the evidence filter matters


Gemini source
Re-scored on Vertex (baseline) or the June rows for 131 re-normalised texts
Provider and text-version sensitivity


Gap legs
Missing model legs left empty (baseline) or filled from June rows
Coverage sensitivity


Parse repair
Keep (baseline) or drop the 363 Claude chunks re-scored after a parser defect
Sensitivity to a repaired defect





Why we run all combinations
A single regression hides the variance across analytic choices. Following Menkveld et al. (2024) “Nonstandard Errors”, we show the distribution of \(\beta\) across the full grid of defensible specifications. If the headline finding (\(\beta < 0\)) holds across thousands of choices, the result is robust to researcher degrees of freedom. The specification curve plot below sorts all selected coefficients; the histogram shows their distribution; the per-fork table decomposes where the variation comes from.

title: Interactive regressions & specification curve
text:
Pick the analytic subfamily

viewof model_set_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["sonnet_only","gpt41_only","gemini_only",
   "sonnet_gpt41","sonnet_gemini","gpt41_gemini","all_three"],
  {value: ["sonnet_only","gpt41_only","gemini_only","sonnet_gpt41","sonnet_gemini","gpt41_gemini","all_three"],
   label: "Model selection (which LLM(s) feed the score)"})

viewof outcome_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["liberalism_overall","lib_political","lib_social","lib_economic","lib_financial_market"],
  {value: ["liberalism_overall"], label: "Outcome dimension"})

viewof within_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["cwm","cwm_pop","mean","median"],
  {value: ["cwm","cwm_pop","mean","median"], label: "Within-manifesto aggregation (cwm = own-block confidence weights, baseline)"})

viewof validation_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["quote","r12","full","none"],
  {value: ["quote","r12","full","none"], label: "Evidence rule (quote = baseline)"})

viewof gemini_pick = Inputs.checkbox(["vertex","june"], {value: ["vertex","june"], label: "Gemini source"})
viewof gap_pick = Inputs.checkbox(["na","june_fallback"], {value: ["na","june_fallback"], label: "Gap legs"})
viewof repair_pick = Inputs.checkbox(["keep","exclude"], {value: ["keep","exclude"], label: "Parse-repaired chunks"})

viewof between_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["mean","median","leave_worst_out"],
  {value: ["mean","median","leave_worst_out"], label: "Between-model aggregation"})

viewof sample_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["full","post2000","post2010","europe_only"],
  {value: ["full","post2000","post2010","europe_only"], label: "Sample restriction"})

viewof fe_pick = Inputs.checkbox(
  ["ctry_year","ctry_year_p","ctry_x_year"],
  {value: ["ctry_year","ctry_year_p","ctry_x_year"], label: "Fixed effects"})








































































filtered = specs.filter(d =>
  model_set_pick.includes(d.model_set) &&
  outcome_pick.includes(d.outcome) &&
  within_pick.includes(d.within_agg) &&
  between_pick.includes(d.between_agg) &&
  sample_pick.includes(d.sample_key) &&
  fe_pick.includes(d.fe_key) &&
  validation_pick.includes(d.validation) &&
  gemini_pick.includes(d.gemini_norm) &&
  gap_pick.includes(d.gap_legs) &&
  repair_pick.includes(d.parse_repaired)
)







outcomeShort = ({
  liberalism_overall: "Liberalism (overall)",
  lib_political: "Political",
  lib_social: "Social",
  lib_economic: "Economic",
  lib_financial_market: "Financial-market"
})
mainSpecs = {
  const hits = outcome_pick.map(o => {
    const h = specs.find(d =>
      d.model_set   === "all_three"   &&
      d.within_agg  === "cwm"         &&
      d.between_agg === "mean"        &&
      d.outcome     === o             &&
      d.sample_key  === "full"        &&
      d.fe_key      === "ctry_year"   &&
      d.validation  === "quote"       &&
      d.gemini_norm === "vertex"      &&
      d.gap_legs    === "na"          &&
      d.parse_repaired === "keep"
    );
    if (h) console.info(`Headline ${o}: β = ${h.coef.toFixed(3)}, p = ${h.p}`);
    return h;
  }).filter(Boolean);
  return hits;
}

title: Interactive regressions & specification curve
Interactive regressions & specification curve
text:
Specification curve

sorted = filtered.map(d => ({...d})).sort((a,b) => a.coef - b.coef)
  .map((d,i) => ({...d, rank: i}))
// For each mainSpec (one per selected outcome), find the rank in the filtered+sorted view
mainInFilter = mainSpecs.flatMap(ms => {
  const r = sorted.find(d =>
    d.model_set   === ms.model_set   &&
    d.within_agg  === ms.within_agg  &&
    d.between_agg === ms.between_agg &&
    d.outcome     === ms.outcome     &&
    d.sample_key  === ms.sample_key  &&
    d.fe_key      === ms.fe_key      &&
    d.validation  === ms.validation  &&
    d.gemini_norm === ms.gemini_norm &&
    d.gap_legs    === ms.gap_legs    &&
    d.parse_repaired === ms.parse_repaired);
  return r ? [r] : [];
})
Plot = await import("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@observablehq/plot@0.6/+esm")
Plot.plot({
  width: 900, height: 380, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Specification (sorted by coefficient)"},
  y: {label: "Populism coefficient"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "grey", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.areaY(sorted, {x: "rank", y1: d => d.coef - 1.96*d.se, y2: d => d.coef + 1.96*d.se, fill: "steelblue", fillOpacity: 0.18}),
    Plot.line(sorted, {x: "rank", y: "coef", stroke: "steelblue", strokeWidth: 1.2}),
    Plot.dot(sorted.filter(d => d.p < 0.05 && d.coef < 0),
      {x: "rank", y: "coef", r: 1.4, fill: "darkgreen", fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.dot(sorted.filter(d => d.coef > 0),
      {x: "rank", y: "coef", r: 2, fill: "red"}),
    // Headline specifications (one ring per selected outcome) + labels
    Plot.dot(mainInFilter, {x: "rank", y: "coef",
        r: 7, fill: "white", stroke: "#cc0033", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(mainInFilter, {x: "rank", y: "coef",
        r: 3, fill: "#cc0033"}),
    Plot.text(mainInFilter, {x: "rank", y: "coef",
        text: d => `${outcomeShort[d.outcome]}: β = ${d.coef.toFixed(3)}`,
        dy: -16, fill: "#cc0033", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: 10,
        textAnchor: "middle"})
  ]
})

Coefficient distribution

Plot.plot({
  width: 900, height: 280, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Populism coefficient"},
  y: {label: "Density"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "grey", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.rectY(filtered, Plot.binX({y: "count"},
      {x: "coef", fill: "steelblue", fillOpacity: 0.6, thresholds: 40})),
    Plot.ruleX([selStats.median], {stroke: "darkblue", strokeWidth: 2}),
    // Headline specs — one vertical red rule + label per selected outcome
    Plot.ruleX(mainInFilter, {x: "coef", stroke: "#cc0033", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.text(mainInFilter, {
      x: "coef",
      text: d => `${outcomeShort[d.outcome]}: ${d.coef.toFixed(3)}`,

title: Interactive regressions & specification curve
Interactive regressions & specification curve
text:
How to read this
This is a specification curve in the sense of Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson (2020) and a multiverse analysis in the sense of Steegen et al. (2016). Following the “non-standard errors” framing of Menkveld et al. (2024), each row of the table above is one defensible analytic choice, and the spread of the coefficients across them measures what the standard error of a single regression cannot: the variance across the analyst’s decision space.

allStats = stats(specs, d => d.coef)
md`Over all **${specs.length.toLocaleString()}** specifications, ${(100*specs.filter(d => d.p < 0.05 && d.coef < 0).length/specs.length).toFixed(1)}% of the populism coefficients are significantly negative and ${specs.filter(d => d.p < 0.05 && d.coef > 0).length} are significantly positive (median ${allStats.median.toFixed(3)}). Filter to your preferred subfamily above to see how the distribution moves; the [results page](../analysis/milei-question.qmd) reports the non-standard errors.`

title: Methodology
text:
Corpus and chunks
The corpus is the Manifesto Project Dataset version 2026a with corpus release 2026-1: 3,371 manifestos with machine-readable text from 62 countries, 1945–2025. A manifesto of at most 18,000 tokens is sent whole; longer ones are split into chunks of 20,000 tokens with a 2,000-token overlap. The texts are © their authors and distributed by the Manifesto Project (WZB); this site does not redistribute them.

title: Methodology
text:
Models
Every chunk is scored by three model families with the same prompt and schema at temperature 0. The version actually served is logged for every call since October 2026; for the June 2026 calls it was not logged. The Gemini June rows used the floating alias gemini-flash-latest, which an anchor test identifies as gemini-3.5-flash.

Methodology

What is scored
Per chunk, each model returns for each of thirteen dimensions a score from 0 to 10 (or none), an evidence status (verified, mixed or no evidence) and a verbatim quote of 3 to 8 words with its surrounding passage.

Range
Definition

title: Methodology
section: From chunk scores to manifesto scores
text:
From chunk scores to manifesto scores

Which chunks count. A chunk’s score enters if the model rates its evidence as verified and the quote passes the quote check: it is found verbatim in the chunk and is not copied from the prompt. Every manifesto page shows each quote and whether it counted.
Within a model: the mean of the counted chunk scores, weighted by the model’s confidence for that block of dimensions (populism, ideology or liberalism).
Across models: the plain mean of the available models. This is the score shown as combined and used in the paper.
Ideology direction: (right − left) / (right + left + centrist) on the combined scores, from −1 (left) to +1 (right).

The site recomputes these scores from the public files and checks that they equal the replication chain’s values exactly before any page is written.

title: Methodology
text:
Robustness
Every defensible alternative (model subsets, within- and between-model aggregation, evidence rules, samples, fixed effects, standard errors) is estimated; the distribution of the populism coefficient over all specifications is the specification curve. Results: the Milei question.

title: Methodology
text:
Evidence on this site
Quotes are shown with their first 8 words and without the surrounding passage, to respect the Manifesto Project’s terms of use. The full model output, including longer quotes and passages, is archived with the replication package and is not public.

title: The Milei question
text:
The question
Javier Milei is widely described as a right-wing populist, and he calls himself a libertarian. Is that a contradiction, or are right-wing populist parties more liberal than populism in general? We score every party manifesto of the Manifesto Project corpus with three large language model families on populism, populist ideology and four kinds of liberalism (political, social, economic, financial-market), and relate the scores in panel regressions with country and year fixed effects.
The corpus holds 3,371 manifestos of 995 parties in 62 countries and 607 elections, 1945–2025; 3,342 have both a populism and a liberalism score. Every score can be checked against its evidence on the manifesto pages.

title: The Milei question
section: Populism goes with less liberalism, on every dimension
text:
Populism goes with less liberalism, on every dimension
A one-point higher populism score goes with a liberalism score that is 0.459 points lower (standard error 0.018, clustered by party; N = 3,340). The relation holds for each liberalism dimension and, smaller, within parties over time (party fixed effects).

title: The Milei question
section: How much do the analytic choices matter?
text:
How much do the analytic choices matter?
Measuring populism with language models involves many defensible choices: which models, how chunk scores are aggregated, which evidence counts, which sample, which fixed effects. We estimate the populism coefficient for every combination: 20,592 distinct specifications, of which 97.9% are significantly negative and none is significantly positive (median -0.310, 95% of estimates between -0.683 and -0.046).

File

Scores and evidence flags: CC-BY 4.0; please cite the paper and the data (below). The manifesto texts are © their authors and distributed by the Manifesto Project (WZB); obtain them there with the manifesto id (doc_id = CMP party code _ election year and month). This site does not redistribute them, and quotes are cut to 8 words.
library(arrow)
scores <- read_parquet("https://populism-llm.org/data/download/manifesto_scores_v2026a.parquet")
# populism_overall, liberalism_overall, lib_political, lib_social, lib_economic,
# lib_financial_market, pop_ideology_direction (-1 left .. +1 right), ...
fixest::feols(liberalism_overall ~ populism_overall | countryname + year, scores, cluster = ~party)
The last line is the paper’s headline regression (column 1 of Table 4).
The exact system prompt, user message and output schema sent to the models are exported from the scoring code with every build: system prompt, user message, schema (see methodology).

title: Data & reproduction
text:
Columns

doc_id, countryname, partyname, partyabbrev, parfam (party family label), party (CMP party code), date, year, token_count.
Thirteen dimensions, 0–10, combined across models: pop_anti_elitism, pop_people_centrism, pop_manichean, populism_overall, pop_ideology_left, pop_ideology_right, pop_ideology_centrist, pop_ideology_overall, lib_political, lib_social, lib_economic, lib_financial_market, liberalism_overall. The same with suffix _sonnet, _gpt41mini, _gemini for each model, and n_models_<dim>.
pop_ideology_direction = (right − left) / (right + left + centrist); the variants _zero, _ge2, _all3 handle missing components differently (robustness).
Provenance: endpoint_<model>, resolved_<model>, share_logged_<model>, aggregation, validation_rule, baseline_version, corpus_version.

CMP coding variables (such as rile) are not included; they are available from the Manifesto Project.

title: Data & reproduction
text:
Reproduction
The paper’s numbers come from one replication chain. It reruns every table and figure from the model output and checks each output file against a recorded checksum. The replication package (code, redacted model output, documentation) will be published with the paper; until then, please contact Sebastian Stöckl.
This site is built from the same chain: it recomputes all scores from the public model output and refuses to build if any score differs from the chain’s value.

text: 🚧 PREVIEW / DRAFT · Working paper, not peer-reviewed. Numbers and methodology may change. Do not cite — sebastian.stoeckl@uni.li.

title: Populism-LLM
text:
Attribute blocks

Populism, populist ideology and liberalism (v2026a (paper baseline)): 13 dimensions. Thirteen dimensions scored on 0–10 by three model families from the full manifesto text, each with a verbatim evidence quote. Scores are aggregated as in Rode & Stöckl (2026): a chunk counts if the model marks its evidence as verified and the quote is found verbatim in the manifesto chunk (and is not copied from the prompt); confidence-weighted mean within model, plain mean across models.

Further blocks, such as a party’s environmental profile or its stance towards democratic institutions, will be added to the same pages as they are scored.
